title: Basic Processing: Introduction
summary: Introduces the idea of writing simple programs that process a small, constant amount of data, similar to calculator operations, and previews a review of constants.
main_text: Basic Processing. To start, we will write programs to do simple processing on a few (a constant amount) of data values. Similar to what you might use a calculator to perform. Let us briefly review the constants we introduced you to in an earlier unit.
notes_text: Sets up the transition into a review of C++ constant/literal types before covering operators.

title: Review: Constants (aka Literals)
summary: Reviews C++ constant/literal types -- integer, double, char, C-strings, and boolean -- including syntax, escape sequences, and how a C-string is laid out in memory with a null terminator.
main_text: Review: Constants (aka Literals). Integer: 496, 10005, -234. Double: 12.0, -16., 0.23, 6.02E23, 4e-2 (both very large and very small numbers, i.e. fractions/decimals). Characters (char type): enclosed in single quotes ('), e.g. 'a', '5', 'B', '!'; each quoted value is converted to the appropriate ASCII number (e.g. 'a' => 97); non-printing special characters use "escape" sequences preceded by a backslash: '\n' (newline/enter), '\t' (tab), '\\' (slash), '\'' (apostrophe). C-Strings (note: there is also a C++ string type): 0 or more characters between double quotes ("), e.g. "hi1\n", "12345", "b", "\tAns. is %d"; ends with a '\0'=0 (aka NULL character) added as the last byte/character to allow code to delimit the end of the string. Boolean (C++ only): false, true; physical representation: 0 = false, non-zero (1, -5, 300) = true.
notes_text: A warning callout notes that C/C++'s handling of single characters and strings differs from most other languages and is a major source of confusion. The memory-layout diagram shows the C-string "hi1\n" stored byte-by-byte at addresses 7420-7426, each byte holding both the ASCII numeric value and the character it represents, ending with the '\0' null terminator at address 7424.

images.description: A memory layout diagram showing the C-string "hi1\n" stored as consecutive bytes at addresses 7420 through 7426, each row listing the address, the numeric (ASCII) value stored, and the corresponding character label (h, i, 1, newline, null terminator '\0', '#', d), illustrating how C-strings are represented in memory and terminated by a null byte.

title: You're Just My Type: Constant Type Matching Exercise
summary: An in-class exercise table asking students to determine whether given C++ constants are correctly matched to a stated type (e.g., 4.0 to int, 'a' to string), with solutions provided later.
main_text: You're Just My Type. Indicate which constants are matched with the correct type. Table pairs: 4.0 -> int; 5 -> int; 'a' -> string; "abc" -> string; 5. -> double; 5 -> char; "5.0" -> double; '5' -> int. Solutions are provided at the end of the slide packet.
notes_text: This is a self-check exercise; the solution slide near the end of the deck (slide 28) reveals which pairings are correct or incorrect and explains each, e.g. 'a' is actually a char (not string) since it uses single quotes, and "abc" is actually a C-string (not the C++ string class) since it uses double quotes without a string variable declaration.

title: Arithmetic Operators
summary: Introduces the basic C++ arithmetic operators (+, -, *, /, %), noting that addition/subtraction/multiplication work for both integer and floating-point types while modulus applies only to integers, with practice problems for modulus.
main_text: Arithmetic Operators. Addition, subtraction, multiplication work as expected for both integer and floating-point types. Modulus is only defined for integers. Operator table: + Addition, - Subtraction, * Multiplication, / Division (Integer vs. Double division), % Modulus (remainder) [for integers only]. Practice: 10 % 3 = __, 17 % 10 = __.
notes_text: Foreshadows the upcoming 'Review: Division' slide by flagging that integer vs. double division behave differently, a distinction covered in more depth two slides later.

title: Precedence: Order of Operations
summary: Explains operator precedence and associativity in C++ expressions using a full precedence table (levels 1-16), with a worked example expression and tips for adding clarity with parentheses and spacing.
main_text: Precedence. Order of operations/evaluation of an expression. Higher levels (e.g. level 16 in table) done first. Notice operations with the same level or precedence usually are evaluated left to right. Evaluate: 2*-4-3+5/2;. Tips: Use parenthesis to add clarity; add a space between literals, e.g. (2 * -4) - 3 + (5 / 2).
notes_text: The referenced precedence table (sourced from https://discuss.codechef.com/upfiles/CPP.PNG) lists 16 precedence levels from scope resolution (highest, level 16) down to the comma operator (lowest, level 1), covering function calls, increment/decrement, multiplicative and additive operators, bitwise shifts, relational/equality operators, bitwise AND/XOR/OR, logical AND/OR, the conditional (ternary) operator, and assignment operators, each annotated with left-to-right or right-to-left associativity.

images.description: A full C++ operator precedence table with columns for Level (1-16), Operators, Description, and Associativity, listing operator categories from scope resolution and function calls (highest precedence) down through unary operators, multiplicative, additive, shift, relational, equality, bitwise, logical, conditional, and assignment operators (lowest precedence), each marked with left-to-right or right-to-left associativity.

title: Review: Integer vs. Floating-Point Division
summary: Explains that C++ division behaves differently depending on operand types: integer division truncates any remainder, while division involving a double produces a fractional result, with operand promotion when mixing types.
main_text: Review: Division. Computers perform division differently based on the type of values used as inputs. Integer Division: When dividing two integral values, the result will also be an integer (any remainder/fraction will be dropped). Examples: 10 / 4 = 2, 52 / 10 = 5, 6 / 7 = 0. Floating-point (Double) & Mixed Division: 10.0 / 4.0 = 2.5, 52.0 / 10 = 5.2, 6 / 7.0 = 0.8571. Note: If one input is a double, the other will be promoted temporarily to compute the result as a double.
notes_text: This is a key gotcha for beginners: dividing two ints (e.g. 10/4) silently truncates to 2 instead of 2.5, while the same numbers as doubles or mixed with a double produce the expected fractional result.

title: Exercise Review: Evaluating Expressions
summary: A practice exercise asking students to evaluate five arithmetic expressions combining integer division, modulus, and floating-point division, with solutions provided later in the deck.
main_text: Exercise Review. Evaluate the following: 25 / 3; 20 - 12 / 4 * 2; 3 - 15 % 7; 18.0 / 4; 28 - 5 / 2.0. Exercises from: D.S. Malik, C++ Programming, 5th Ed., Ch. 2, Q6.
notes_text: Solutions appear later in the deck (slide 29): 25/3 = 8, 20-12/4*2 = 14, 3-15%7 = 2, 18.0/4 = 2.5, 28-5/2.0 = 25.5 -- each testing precedence, integer truncation, and modulus together.

title: Section Divider: Output
summary: Section header slide introducing the C++ output topic, transitioning from operators to writing programs that display results with cout.
main_text: OUTPUT
notes_text: Marks the start of the cout/output-focused portion of the unit.

title: Scalar Processing Programs: The (P)IPO Pattern
summary: Introduces the (Prompt)-Input-Process-Output pattern that scalar processing programs generally follow, with four concrete example program transcripts and a note on the meaning of 'scalar' in this context.
main_text: Scalar Processing Programs. A real program needs to get input values and produce output (text to the screen). These scalar processing programs generally follow a simple sequence: (Prompt)-Input-Process-Output (P)IPO. 1. Prompt the user for 1 or more (some constant amount of) input values. 2. Receive the input value(s). 3. Using the input, perform operations (processing) to produce 1 or more (some constant amount of) desired output values. 4. Display the output value(s). Note: A scalar (in this context) refers to 1, 2, or some small constant number of input values (as opposed to a variable number of input values).
notes_text: The three example terminal transcripts (eggs-to-dozens, tuition calculation, rectangle/triangle area) are each numbered 1 (prompt), 2 (input), 4 (output) but conspicuously omit a visible step 3, prompting the rhetorical question 'Where is the processing?' -- highlighting that processing happens invisibly inside the program between input and output.

images.description: Three annotated terminal transcripts illustrating the Prompt-Input-Process-Output pattern: an egg-to-dozens converter, a tuition cost calculator, and a rectangle/triangle area calculator. Each transcript's prompt line is labeled '1', the user's typed input is labeled '2', and the final output line is labeled '4', with no visible label '3' for processing, prompting the caption 'Where is the processing?'
labels: How many eggs do you have?

title: C++ Output: The cout Command
summary: Introduces 'cout' (character output) as the basic C++ command for printing to the screen, with a minimal 'Hello' example and a diagram of how cout sends data through the OS to the display.
main_text: C++ Output. The most basic programming command is usually printing something to the screen. In C++, this is done with a cout (short for character output) command. Note: 'endl' stands for end-line and causes the cursor to move to the next line of the screen, similar to '\n'.
notes_text: The accompanying diagram traces the flow of the string "Hello" from the cout command, through the operating system (OS), and finally rendered on the monitor screen, reinforcing that output is not instantaneous magic but flows through a defined path.

images.description: A flow diagram showing a C++ program's 'cout << "Hello" << endl;' statement flowing down through a labeled 'cout' bubble as an 'output stream', then through the OS, and finally appearing as the text 'Hello' on a computer monitor icon.

title: Output From Your Program: Computing vs. Printing
summary: Contrasts merely computing a value (which produces no visible output) with explicitly printing it using cout, using a 'thought vs. speech' analogy and two side-by-side code examples.
main_text: Output From Your Program. There's a difference between thinking something and saying it! To see output in C++ we need to explicitly tell the computer to output the value using 'cout'. Just computing it is not good enough.
notes_text: Left code example computes '12 * 3;' as a standalone statement with no output produced; right code example wraps the same computation in 'cout << 12 * 3 << endl;' which prints '36' to the screen -- illustrated with a 'thinking' emoji (no output) versus a 'writing it down' emoji (output produced).

images.description: Two side-by-side C++ code panels each paired with a blank vs. filled computer monitor: the left panel shows '12 * 3;' as a bare statement producing no printed result (monitor stays blank), illustrated with a thinking-face emoji labeled 'Performing computation is like having a thought. No output is generated unless you explicitly write it down.'; the right panel shows 'cout << 12 * 3 << endl;' printing '36' to the monitor, illustrated with a writing emoji labeled 'To output a result to the screen in C++ (i.e. "write it down") we use the cout command.'
labels: Performing computation is like having a thought
To output a result to the screen

title: Printing Different Values & Types with cout
summary: Explains that cout requires the '<<' stream insertion operator as a separator between values and does not add spaces automatically, illustrated with several output variations and a note on the overloaded meaning of '<<'.
main_text: Printing Different Values & Types. 'cout' requires appropriate use of separators between consecutive values or different types of values. 'cout' does not add spaces between consecutive values; you must do so explicitly. Since text strings are a different value we must separate it with the '<<' operator. Generally good practice to give some descriptive text with your numeric output. Note: You may divide up output over multiple cout statements. Unless an 'endl' or '\n' is used, the next cout statement will resume where the last one left off.
notes_text: The example code shows a compile error from omitting '<<' between two numbers ('cout << 102 1889 << endl;'), then progressively better versions adding '<<' and an explicit space string, producing outputs '1021889', '102 1889', '102 1889', and 'There are 525600 minutes in a year.' A callout explains that '<<' is 'overloaded': in C it means bit-shift-left, but in C++'s output context it is the 'stream insertion' operator instead.

images.description: A C++ code panel showing four progressively corrected cout statements printing two adjacent numbers -- first causing a compile error from a missing '<<' operator, then compiling but with no space, then with an explicit space string for readability, then as a single combined string -- followed by console output showing the resulting differences, with a callout box explaining that '<<' is the overloaded 'stream insertion' operator in C++'s output context (versus the bitwise left-shift operator in C).
labels: There are 525600 minutes in a year.

title: Section Divider: Variables and Receiving Input with cin
summary: Section header slide transitioning from output topics to variables and keyboard input using cin.
main_text: VARIABLES AND RECEIVING INPUT WITH CIN
notes_text: Marks the shift from cout/output to variable declarations and cin/input handling for the remainder of the unit.

title: The Need For Variables & Input
summary: Motivates variables and user input by noting that printing hardcoded constants is inflexible; variables let programs store/name values while cin lets programs work for arbitrary user-provided input, contrasted with a fixed-constant version.
main_text: The Need For Variables & Input. Printing out constants is not very useful (nor exciting). In fact, we could just as easily compute the value ourselves in many situations. The real power of computation comes when we introduce variables and user input via cin. Variables provide the ability to store/remember a value and also give that value a name. User input allows us to write general programs that work for "any" input values. Thus, a more powerful program would allow us to enter an arbitrary number and perform conversion to dozens.
notes_text: Two code examples are contrasted: one hardcodes '3*12' to always convert exactly 3 dozen, while the other declares an 'int numDozen' variable and uses 'cin >> numDozen' to read a user-supplied count, generalizing the dozens-to-items conversion. Note the second example's source has a minor inconsistency: it declares 'numDozen' but the cout statement references an undeclared variable 'dozen'.

title: C/C++ Variables: Declaration, Assignment, and Memory
summary: Defines a variable as a reserved, named memory location that stores a value, explains the declaration syntax 'type name = initial_value;', and shows how declaring/assigning/using numDozen maps to actual bytes in RAM.
main_text: C/C++ Variables. A variable is a reserved location of memory and associates a descriptive name (e.g. numDozen) with that location and stores a value (int, double, char, etc.) that can be used or changed. You must "declare" (allocate) your variables before using them. Syntax: type name = initial_value; (e.g. int numDozen = 3;). It's like renting an apartment or storage unit -- you must rent the apartment before moving your stuff in.
notes_text: The code example declares 'int numDozen = 3;', prints 'numDozen * 12' (36), reassigns 'numDozen = 5;', and prints again (60). The memory diagram shows numDozen occupying 4 bytes at address 1000, holding the value 00000003 and later being overwritten to 00000005, annotated to note an int is a 4-byte variable and that variables are only actually allocated in RAM when the program runs.

images.description: A diagram of computer memory (RAM) showing a table of addresses (1000-1008+) and their stored byte values, with the 4-byte int variable 'numDozen' highlighted at address 1000 holding the hex value 00000003, and an arrow noting an int occupies 4 bytes; paired with a code panel where 'declare', 'use', 'assign', and 'use' steps are each pointed out for the statements int numDozen = 3;, cout << numDozen * 12, numDozen = 5;, and cout << numDozen * 12 again, producing console output 36 then 60.
labels: A picture of computer memory (aka RAM)
Variables are actually allocated in RAM when the program is run

title: Keyboard Input: The cin Object
summary: Explains that 'cin' receives keyboard input via an OS-managed input stream and extracts/converts text into a variable's type, illustrated with an eggs-per-dozen example and a flow diagram.
main_text: Keyboard Input. In C++, the 'cin' object is responsible for receiving input from the keyboard. Keyboard input is captured and stored by the OS (in an "input stream") until cin is called upon to "extract" info into a variable in your program. 'cin' converts text input to desired format (e.g. integer, double, etc.).
notes_text: A callout notes that a variable's value is random garbage until it is initialized, either by assignment or by a cin read. The flow diagram traces keystrokes '1', '5', '\n' typed on the keyboard, through the OS into an input stream, then extracted by cin into the 'dozens' variable (value 15), leaving the trailing '\n' behind in the stream.

images.description: A flow diagram showing keystrokes '1', '5', newline typed on a keyboard, passing through the OS into an 'input stream' bubble, and then extracted by 'cin' into the program's 'dozens' variable (shown transitioning from '??' uninitialized garbage to the value 15), with the leftover newline character remaining in the input stream.
labels: A variable's value is random garbage until you initialize it

title: Dealing With Whitespace in cin
summary: Explains how cin handles whitespace: it skips leading whitespace, reads until the first trailing whitespace or an unconvertible character, and leaves the rest in the stream for the next cin call.
main_text: Dealing With Whitespace. Whitespace (def.): Characters that represent horizontal or vertical blank space. Examples: newline ('\n'), TAB ('\t'), spacebar (' '). cin sequentially discards leading whitespace characters until it hits a non-whitespace. cin then checks the characters can be converted to the appropriate variable type and keeps scanning for more. cin will STOP at the first trailing whitespace (or on a character unable to be converted to the desired type) and await the next cin command. Main Take-aways: cin SKIPS leading whitespace; cin STOPS on the first trailing whitespace; Space is not equal to Whitespace in general usage here (Whitespace = ' ', '\t', '\n', etc., all count).
notes_text: Worked example: user types tab, '1', '5', newline; cin skips the leading tab, reads '1' then '5' as digits, stops at the trailing newline, and extracts the integer 15 into 'dozens', leaving the newline in the input stream for a subsequent read.

images.description: A flow diagram showing a user typing tab, '1', '5', newline at the keyboard; the input stream retains these characters until cin skips the leading tab, extracts '15' into the 'dozens' variable, and stops at the trailing newline, which remains in the input stream awaiting the next cin call.
labels: Suppose at the prompt the user types
cin STOPS on the first trailing whitespace

title: Multiple Inputs and Unexpected Inputs
summary: Shows chaining the '>>' extraction operator to read several variables in one cin statement, and notes the (temporary) simplifying assumption that user input is always correctly formatted.
main_text: Multiple Inputs and Unexpected Inputs. Use the '>>' operator to separate any number of variables you want to read. For now, let us make the unreasonable assumption that the user always types in the right "format" of information. We'll learn more about how cin handles errors later.
notes_text: Example reads an int 'score' and a double 'multiplier' in one statement ('cin >> score >> multiplier;') from input '15 2.4', producing output 'Your new score is 36'. A callout again notes that '>>' is overloaded: in C it is the bitwise right-shift operator, but in C++'s input context it is the "stream extraction" operator.

images.description: A flow diagram showing keyboard input '15 2.4' passing through an input stream and being extracted by a single chained cin statement ('cin >> score >> multiplier;') into two separate variables, an int 'score' (15) and a double 'multiplier' (2.4), producing console output 'Your new score is 36'.

title: Timing of Execution: When cin Waits vs. Extracts Immediately
summary: Explains that a cin statement will either wait for the user to type and press Enter (if the input stream is empty) or immediately extract already-buffered text without waiting, illustrated with a two-variable (dozens, gpa) example.
main_text: Timing of Execution. When execution reaches a 'cin' statement, it will either: Wait for input if nothing is available in the input stream (the OS will capture what is typed until the next 'Enter' key is hit; the user can type as little or much as desired until Enter). Immediately extract from the input stream if some text is available and convert it to the desired type of data.
notes_text: The example has the user type '15 3.7' followed by Enter all at once. The first 'cin >> dozens;' waits (since the stream starts empty) and extracts 15, leaving '3.7\n' behind. The second 'cin >> gpa;' then does NOT wait, since '3.7' is already sitting in the input stream, and immediately extracts 3.7 into gpa.

images.description: A flow diagram tracing a single line of typed input '15 3.7\n' through two separate cin statements: the first ('cin >> dozens;') waits for the Enter key since the input stream starts empty, then extracts 15 into 'dozens'; the second ('cin >> gpa;') does not wait because '3.7\n' is already buffered in the input stream, and immediately extracts 3.7 into 'gpa'.
labels: No input available. Wait for user to type and hit Enter

title: Challenge 1: Processing and Output Practice
summary: A coding challenge asking students to write a program that incorporates processing and output (without prompting/input) for a fixed input, exemplified by a speed/distance/time conversion.
main_text: Challenge 1. Write a program that incorporates: Processing; Output. Think of simple converters/calculator operations to work with a fixed input. Example: How many hours will it take to drive 850 miles at 110 km/h?
notes_text: This challenge deliberately omits Prompt and Input, focusing students on hardcoding a fixed value, computing a result, and displaying it with cout -- setting up the fuller Prompt-Input-Process-Output exercise in Challenge 2.

title: Challenge 2: Full Prompt-Input-Process-Output Practice
summary: A coding challenge asking students to write a program using all four (P)IPO stages -- prompt, input, processing, and output -- exemplified by computing distance fallen under gravity given initial velocity and time.
main_text: Challenge 2. Write a program that incorporates all 3 aspects: Prompt; Input; Processing; Output. Example: Compute and output how far an object with initial downward velocity, v, has fallen after t seconds?
notes_text: Builds directly on Challenge 1 by adding the Prompt and Input stages using cin, requiring a full (P)IPO program rather than one with a hardcoded value.

title: You're Just My Type: Solutions
summary: Provides the answer key for the earlier constant-type-matching exercise, explaining why each pairing is right or wrong, e.g. distinguishing char vs. C-string vs. the C++ string class.
main_text: You're Just My Type (Solutions). 4.0 -> int: Wrong, it's a double (has a decimal point). 5 -> int: Right. 'a' -> string: Wrong, it's a char (single quotes). "abc" -> string: Wrong, it's a C-string (double quotes, not the C++ string class). 5. -> double: Right, a float/double since it has a decimal indicator. 5 -> char: Wrong, it's an int, though it could validly be stored in a char variable since a char is just a number that fits in 8 bits/1 byte. "5.0" -> double: Wrong, it's a C-string. '5' -> int: Wrong, it's a char.
notes_text: Reinforces the core distinctions from the Review: Constants slide -- single quotes always denote char, double quotes always denote a C-string literal (not the separate C++ string class), and a trailing decimal point denotes a double even without digits after it.

title: Exercise Review: Solutions
summary: Provides the worked answers to the earlier expression-evaluation exercise covering integer division, modulus, and floating-point division.
main_text: Exercise Review (Solutions). 25 / 3 = 8. 20 - 12 / 4 * 2 = 14. 3 - 15 % 7 = 2. 18.0 / 4 = 2.5. 28 - 5 / 2.0 = 25.5. Exercises from: D.S. Malik, C++ Programming, 5th Ed., Ch. 2, Q6.
notes_text: Each answer demonstrates operator precedence and integer-vs-double division rules from earlier slides: e.g. '20 - 12 / 4 * 2' evaluates division and multiplication left-to-right before subtraction (12/4=3, 3*2=6, 20-6=14).

title: The Need For Variables & Input (Backup Version)
summary: An alternate version of the variables/input motivation slide, showing full, executable code for both the fixed-constant version and the cin-based general version of the dozens-to-items example.
main_text: The Need For Variables & Input. Printing out constants is not very useful (nor exciting). In fact, we could just as easily compute the value ourselves in many situations. The real power of computation comes when we introduce variables and user input via cin. Variables provide the ability to store/remember a value and also give that value a name. title: C/C++ Variables (Backup Version): Declaration Rules and Memory Layout
summary: An alternate, more detailed version of the C/C++ variables slide, covering declaration rules (declare-before-use, type+name required), a char/int memory layout example, and a C-vs-C++ difference callout about where declarations must appear.
main_text: C/C++ Variables. A variable is a reserved memory location that stores a value that can be read (retrieved) or written (changed) as often as desired, and associates a descriptive name (e.g. numDozen) the programmer will use with that memory location (aka address) and the value stored in that location. It's like renting an apartment or storage unit. You must "declare" (allocate) your variables before using/assigning to them. A variable is not allocated (aka "in scope") until the computer executes the line with the declaration. The declaration must give the type of the variable and a name/identifier.
notes_text: A callout box highlights a key C vs. C++ difference: C required all variables to be declared at the beginning of a function before any operations, while C++ relaxes this and allows declarations anywhere in the code. The code example shows an invalid use-before-declare ('gr = 'A'; // BAD!') followed by the corrected 'char gr = 'A';', plus an uninitialized 'int x;' later assigned 'x = 1;'. The memory diagram shows 'char gr' as a single byte (binary 01000010, i.e. 'B' after reassignment) and 'int x' as four contiguous bytes, illustrating relative variable sizes in RAM.
